claim: Mannose has anticancer activity that inhibits cell proliferation and enhances the efficacy of chemotherapy.
source: Mannose has anticancer activity that inhibits cell proliferation and enhances the efficacy of chemotherapy.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known property of mannose, supported by the citation to Gonzalez et al., 2018 in the introduction.

claim: The large influx of mannose exceeding its metabolic capacity induced metabolic remodeling, leading to the generation of slow-cycling cells with limited deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates (dNTPs).
source: Here, using genetically engineered human cancer cells that permit the precise control of mannose metabolic flux, we demonstrate that the large influx of mannose exceeding its metabolic capacity induced metabolic remodeling, leading to the generation of slow-cycling cells with limited deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates (dNTPs).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data from metabolomics, cell cycle analysis, and dNTP measurements presented in Figures 2, 5, and 6.

claim: Metabolic remodeling by mannose impaired dormant origin firing required to rescue stalled forks by cisplatin, thus exacerbating replication stress.
source: This metabolic remodeling impaired dormant origin firing required to rescue stalled forks by cisplatin, thus exacerbating replication stress.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in Figure 4 showing BrdU incorporation, RPA2 phosphorylation, and γH2AX levels.

claim: Pharmacological inhibition of de novo dNTP biosynthesis was sufficient to retard cell cycle progression, sensitize cells to cisplatin, and inhibit dormant origin firing.
source: Importantly, pharmacological inhibition of de novo dNTP biosynthesis was sufficient to retard cell cycle progression, sensitize cells to cisplatin, and inhibit dormant origin firing, suggesting dNTP loss-induced genomic instability as a central mechanism for the anticancer activity of mannose.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in Figure 7 using hydroxyurea treatment.

claim: MPI catalyzes the interconversion between fructose-6-phosphate (Fruc-6-P) and mannose-6-phosphate (Man-6-P).
source: This process requires the action of mannose phosphate isomerase (MPI), the enzyme that catalyzes the interconversion between fructose-6-phosphate (Fruc-6-P) and mannose-6-phosphate (Man-6-P) (Alton et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Alton et al., 1998 and is established scientific knowledge.

claim: Man-6-P is converted to GDP-mannose for the biosynthesis of asparagine-linked glycans (N-glycans) in the endoplasmic reticulum.
source: Man-6-P is further converted to GDP-mannose for the biosynthesis of asparagine-linked glycans (N-glycans) in the endoplasmic reticulum (Harada et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Harada et al., 2013.

claim: Extracellular mannose concentration in blood is 30–130 μM.
source: In the secretory pathway, extensive trimming of N-glycans by mannosidases generates free mannose, which is secreted from cells and contributes to the extracellular pool of mannose (30–130 μM in blood) (Sharma and Freeze, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sharma and Freeze, 2011.

claim: The majority of salvaged mannose is efficiently directed into glycolysis by the action of MPI.
source: The extracellular mannose can be taken up by cells and the salvaged mannose is directly converted to Man-6-P, the majority of which is efficiently directed into glycolysis by the action of MPI for unknown reasons (Ichikawa et al., 2014; Sharma and Freeze, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ichikawa et al., 2014 and Sharma and Freeze, 2011.

claim: The large influx of mannose suppresses cell proliferation and enhances the efficacy of chemotherapy, particularly in cancer cells that express low levels of MPI.
source: The large influx of mannose is known to suppress cell proliferation and enhance the efficacy of chemotherapy, particularly in cancer cells that express low levels of MPI (Gonzalez et al., 2018), although the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gonzalez et al., 2018.

claim: Feeding mannose to honeybees is lethal to these insects.
source: It has been known for nearly a century that feeding mannose to honeybees, which are believed to express negligible amounts of MPI (Sols et al., 1960), is lethal to these insects (Staudenmayer, 1939).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sols et al., 1960 and Staudenmayer, 1939.

claim: In honeybees, intracellular levels of Man-6-P exceed the capacity to metabolize it, and the excess Man-6-P inhibits glucose metabolism and decreases the intracellular ATP pool.
source: This is because the intracellular levels of Man-6-P exceed the capacity to metabolize it, and the excess Man-6-P inhibits glucose metabolism and decreases the intracellular ATP pool (DeRossi et al., 2006; Sols et al., 1960).
evidence: This is supported by citations to DeRossi et al., 2006 and Sols et al., 1960.

claim: The addition of 50 μM mannose (unchallenged) to culture medium supported the proliferation of MPI-KO MEFs.
source: The addition of a physiological concentration of mannose (50 μM, unchallenged) to culture medium supported the proliferation of MPI-KO MEFs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Mannose starvation or the addition of 5 mM mannose (challenged) suppressed the proliferation of MPI-KO MEFs, but not that of wild-type MEFs.
source: In contrast, mannose starvation or the addition of a supraphysiological concentration of mannose (5 mM, challenged) suppressed the proliferation of MPI-KO MEFs, but not that of wild-type MEFs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Three MPI-KO HT1080 clones were obtained.
source: Three MPI-KO HT1080 clones were obtained (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: In MPI-KO HT1080 clone #1, cell division stopped under mannose-unchallenged conditions.
source: In one clone (#1), cell division stopped under mannose-unchallenged conditions, but the other two clones (#2 and #3) could proliferate.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental results.

claim: MPI-KO HT1080 clones #2 and #3 exhibited mannose auxotrophy and sensitivity.
source: These two clones exhibited mannose auxotrophy and sensitivity as expected (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and B)
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: Parental HT1080 cells showed marginal defects in cell proliferation at mannose concentrations higher than 15 mM.
source: while the parental HT1080 cells showed marginal defects in cell proliferation at mannose concentrations higher than 15 mM (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The effects of mannose starvation and mannose challenge on the proliferation of MPI-KO cells were almost fully rescued by reintroduction of the human MPI gene.
source: The effects of mannose starvation and mannose challenge on the proliferation of MPI-KO cells were almost fully rescued by reintroduction of the human MPI gene (Figure 1D–F and Figure 1—figure supplement 2C–E), ruling out the potential off-target effects of gene editing.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1D–F and Figure 1—figure supplement 2C–E.

claim: Mannose challenge to MPI-KO HT1080 cells caused the dramatic accumulation of hexose-6-phosphate compared with that under mannose-unchallenged conditions.
source: As expected, mannose challenge to MPI-KO HT1080 cells caused the dramatic accumulation of hexose-6-phosphate (the sum of glucose-6-phosphate and Man-6-P) compared with that under mannose-unchallenged conditions (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by metabolomic data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Mannose starvation severely decreased N-glycosylation in MPI-KO HT1080 cells.
source: Consistent with the essential role of exogenous mannose in the production of Man-6-P and therefore that of GDP-mannose for N-glycan biosynthesis in MPI-KO MEFs (Harada et al., 2013), mannose starvation severely decreased N-glycosylation in MPI-KO HT1080 cells (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is supported by lectin blot data shown in Figure 1H and citation to Harada et al., 2013.

claim: Mannose challenge showed negligible effects on N-glycosylation in MPI-KO HT1080 cells.
source: However, mannose challenge showed negligible effects on N-glycosylation, indicating that mannose challenge suppresses cell proliferation through a mechanism distinct from N-glycosylation defects.
evidence: This is inferred from the lectin blot data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Mannose challenge increased the sensitivity of MPI-KO HT1080 cells to DNA replication inhibitors (cisplatin and doxorubicin) when the cells had been preconditioned with excess mannose prior to the drug treatment.
source: Mannose challenge increased the sensitivity of MPI-KO HT1080 cells to DNA replication inhibitors (i.e., cisplatin and doxorubicin) when the cells had been preconditioned with excess mannose prior to the drug treatment (Figure 1I and J and Figure 1—figure supplement 2F and G).
evidence: This is supported by cell viability assay data shown in Figure 1I and J and Figure 1—figure supplement 2F and G.

claim: Mannose challenge also increased the sensitivity of MPI-KO HeLa cells to cisplatin and doxorubicin.
source: We also generated MPI-KO HeLa cells as another cell model (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–I) and found that mannose challenge also increased the sensitivity of these cells to cisplatin and doxorubicin (Figure 1—figure supplement 3J and K).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3J and K.

claim: Under mannose-unchallenged conditions, MPI-KO HT1080 cells showed exponential growth and a typical Fucci(CA) signal profile.
source: Under mannose-unchallenged conditions, MPI-KO HT1080 cells showed exponential growth (Figure 2C) and a typical Fucci(CA) signal profile (Figure 2B and D), as reported in HeLa cells (Sakaue-Sawano et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 2B, C, and D, and citation to Sakaue-Sawano et al., 2017.

claim: Mannose challenge almost completely suppressed cell proliferation and significantly prolonged the cell cycle.
source: In contrast, mannose challenge almost completely suppressed cell proliferation (Figure 2C) and significantly prolonged the cell cycle, showing a variety of atypical Fucci(CA) signal profiles (Figure 2E and F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 2C, E, F, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: A small proportion (12%) of the mannose-challenged cells showed normal-like but strikingly extended Fucci(CA) signal profiles.
source: The classification analysis revealed that a small proportion of the mannose-challenged cells showed normal-like but strikingly extended Fucci(CA) signal profiles (Figure 2E and F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, normal-like, 12% of the total).
evidence: This is supported by classification analysis of Fucci(CA) profiles shown in Figure 2E, F, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Normal-like mannose-challenged cell populations frequently failed to undergo cytokinesis in M phase and re-entered G1 phase without generating two equivalent daughter cells.
source: Notably, these normal-like cell populations frequently failed to undergo cytokinesis in M phase and re-entered G1 phase without generating two equivalent daughter cells (Video 2).
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse video data shown in Video 2.

claim: 26.7% of mannose-challenged cells were arrested in G1 phase.
source: Other fractions included cells that were arrested in G1 phase (Figure 2E and F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, RRR, 26.7%)
evidence: This is supported by classification analysis shown in Figure 2E, F, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: 40.6% of mannose-challenged cells showed little to no double-positive phase (i.e., the G2-to-M phase).
source: that showed little to no double-positive phase (i.e., the G2-to-M phase) (Figure 2E and F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, RGR, 15.8% and GRG, 9.9%, GDn, 5.9%, RGG, 5.0%, RGDn, 4.0%; 40.6% of total)
evidence: This is supported by classification analysis shown in Figure 2E, F, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: 8.9% of mannose-challenged cells remained in the double-negative phase.
source: or that remained in the double-negative phase (Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, Dn, 8.9%), which is normally seen only at the G1/S transition (Sakaue-Sawano et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by classification analysis shown in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, and citation to Sakaue-Sawano et al., 2017.

claim: Switching of the mannose-challenge medium to the mannose-unchallenged medium after long-term mannose challenge (6 d) resulted in robust cell proliferation.
source: Strikingly, however, switching of the mannose-challenge medium to the mannose-unchallenged medium after long-term mannose challenge (6 d) resulted in robust cell proliferation (Figure 2G) with cell cycle progression indistinguishable from that of mannose-unchallenged cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–D), suggesting that some fraction of the mannose-challenged cells had entered a quiescent state upon mannose challenge.
evidence: This is supported by cell proliferation data shown in Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–D.

claim: Mannose challenge induced early accumulation of the cell cycle inhibitors p21 and p27.
source: Supporting this assumption, mannose challenge induced early accumulation of the cell cycle inhibitors p21 and p27 (Abukhdeir and Park, 2008; Figure 2H).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2H and citation to Abukhdeir and Park, 2008.

claim: BrdU was incorporated into DNA in both mannose-challenged and -unchallenged cells, but mannose challenge gradually decreased cell populations that were actively synthesizing DNA over the incubation time.
source: BrdU was incorporated into DNA in both mannose-challenged and -unchallenged cells, but mannose challenge gradually decreased cell populations that were actively synthesizing DNA over the incubation time (Figure 2I and J).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2I and J.

claim: Small proportions of the mannose-challenged cells exhibited DNA content greater than 4n after 2-day mannose challenge, which also exhibited BrdU incorporation, suggesting that these cell populations underwent endoreplication.
source: Small proportions of the mannose-challenged cells exhibited DNA content greater than 4n after 2-day mannose challenge, which also exhibited BrdU incorporation, suggesting that these cell populations underwent endoreplication (Edgar and Orr-Weaver, 2001).
evidence: This is inferred from flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2I and supported by citation to Edgar and Orr-Weaver, 2001.

claim: Functional annotation analysis of the proteomic data revealed the downregulation of proteins related to the cell cycle and DNA replication in mannose-challenged cells.
source: Functional annotation analysis of the proteomic data using DAVID bioinformatic resources (https://david.ncifcrf.gov) revealed the downregulation of proteins related to the cell cycle and DNA replication in mannose-challenged cells (Figure 3A), which were enriched with the mini-chromosome maintenance 2-7 (MCM2-7) complex (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by proteomic data analysis shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: Mannose challenge decreased the expression levels of MCM2-7 proteins and their genes during mannose challenge over 6 d.
source: Western blot analysis and quantitative polymerase chain reaction (qPCR) confirmed the decrease in the expression levels of MCM2-7 proteins (Figure 3C) and their genes (Figure 3D) during mannose challenge over 6 d.
evidence: This is supported by western blot and qPCR data shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: The MCM2-7 complex is a core component of DNA helicase that unwinds the DNA duplex at replication forks in S phase.
source: The MCM2-7 complex is a core component of DNA helicase that unwinds the DNA duplex at replication forks in S phase (Jones et al., 2021; Rzechorzek et al., 2020)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Jones et al., 2021 and Rzechorzek et al., 2020.

claim: The MCM2-7 complex plays a central role in the licensing of replication origins in G1 phase by forming a pre-replicative complex with the six-subunit origin recognition complex (ORC1-6), CDC6, and CDT1 on chromatin.
source: and the complex also plays a central role in the licensing of replication origins in G1 phase by forming a pre-replicative complex with the six-subunit origin recognition complex (ORC1-6), CDC6, and CDT1 on chromatin (Frigola et al., 2017; Remus et al., 2009; Zhai et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Frigola et al., 2017, Remus et al., 2009, and Zhai et al., 2017.

claim: CDC6 and CDT1 were depleted after 2-day mannose challenge, whereas the ORC2 subunit was expressed at relatively constant levels.
source: CDC6 and CDT1, which were not detected in our proteomic analysis, were depleted after 2-day mannose challenge, whereas the ORC2 subunit was expressed at relatively constant levels (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Under the mannose-unchallenged conditions, the binding of MCM2 to chromatin took place in G1 phase and peaked at the G1/S boundary in MPI-KO HT1080 cells and MPI-KO HeLa cells, indicating that replication origins were fully licensed.
source: Under the mannose-unchallenged conditions, the binding of MCM2 to chromatin took place in G1 phase (Figure 3E, step i) and peaked at the G1/S boundary (Figure 3E, step ii) in MPI-KO HT1080 cells and MPI-KO HeLa cells, indicating that replication origins were fully licensed (Matson et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by chromatin flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3E and citation to Matson et al., 2017.

claim: Mannose challenge did not severely impair origin licensing, but caused the accumulation of MCM2-positive chromatin in S phase.
source: Mannose challenge did not severely impair origin licensing (Figure 3E, step i), but the same treatment caused the accumulation of MCM2-positive chromatin in S phase (Figure 3E, step iii).
evidence: This is supported by chromatin flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The mannose-challenged cells were not actively incorporating BrdU into DNA.
source: Notably, the mannose-challenged cells were not actively incorporating BrdU into DNA (Figure 2I and J and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that ongoing replication forks were stuck on chromatin with little DNA synthesis under the mannose-challenged conditions.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2I and J and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: In humans, replication origins are licensed far more than actually used for DNA replication.
source: In humans, replication origins are licensed far more than actually used for DNA replication (Langley et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Langley et al., 2016.

claim: The excess origins remain dormant under physiological conditions, while the dormant origins are activated for DNA replication when nearby replication forks stall upon encountering DNA lesions, thus preventing cells from the permanent replication arrest that leads to cell death.
source: The excess origins remain dormant under physiological conditions, while the dormant origins are activated for DNA replication when nearby replication forks stall upon encountering DNA lesions, thus preventing cells from the permanent replication arrest that leads to cell death (Blow et al., 2011; Ge et al., 2007; Kawabata et al., 2011; Shima et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Blow et al., 2011, Ge et al., 2007, Kawabata et al., 2011, and Shima et al., 2007.

claim: In the mannose-unchallenged MPI-KO HT1080 cells and MPI-KO HeLa cells, the cisplatin treatment alone partially suppressed the incorporation of BrdU, which was greatly recovered by ATR inhibition with VE-821 (ATRi), indicating that dormant origins are present in excess and their activation can engage in DNA synthesis during replication stress.
source: In the mannose-unchallenged MPI-KO HT1080 cells (Figure 4B and C) and MPI-KO HeLa cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B), the cisplatin treatment alone partially suppressed the incorporation of BrdU, which was greatly recovered by ATR inhibition with VE-821 (ATRi) (Charrier et al., 2011; Prevo et al., 2012; Reaper et al., 2011), indicating that dormant origins are present in excess and their activation can engage in DNA synthesis during replication stress.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4B and C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B, and citations to Charrier et al., 2011, Prevo et al., 2012, and Reaper et al., 2011.

claim: In the mannose-challenged cells, the cisplatin treatment more severely reduced BrdU incorporation, which was barely restored by ATRi treatment.
source: In the mannose-challenged cells, however, the cisplatin treatment more severely reduced BrdU incorporation, which was barely restored by ATRi treatment (Figure 4B and C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4B and C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Forced activation of dormant origins during replication stress causes the uncoupling of DNA unwinding and synthesis, leading to the accumulation of single-stranded DNA on chromatin marked by phosphorylation of the replication protein A2 (RPA2).
source: Forced activation of dormant origins during replication stress is known to cause the uncoupling of DNA unwinding and synthesis (Murai et al., 2018), leading to the accumulation of single-stranded DNA on chromatin marked by phosphorylation of the replication protein A2 (RPA2) (Figure 4D), confirming the activation of dormant origins by ATRi treatment in both mannose-challenged and -unchallenged cells.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4D and citation to Murai et al., 2018.

claim: The replication initiation step requires chromatin loading of cell division cycle 45 (CDC45), one of the essential and limiting factors for replication initiation, while this process was not severely impaired by mannose challenge.
source: The replication initiation step requires chromatin loading of cell division cycle 45 (CDC45), one of the essential and limiting factors for replication initiation (Moyer et al., 2006), while this process was not severely impaired by mannose challenge (Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A and B, and citation to Moyer et al., 2006.

claim: Under mannose-unchallenged conditions, cisplatin treatment induced the unloading of CDC45 from chromatin, which was restored by the forced activation of dormant origins.
source: Under mannose-unchallenged conditions, cisplatin treatment induced the unloading of CDC45 from chromatin, which was restored by the forced activation of dormant origins (Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: Mannose challenge abrogated the CDC45 unloading/reloading dynamics under replication stress conditions.
source: However, mannose challenge abrogated the CDC45 unloading/reloading dynamics under replication stress conditions (Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: The deficiency in the DNA synthesis from dormant origins and the CDC45 dynamics was associated with the increase in cisplatin-induced γH2AX.
source: The deficiency in the DNA synthesis from dormant origins and the CDC45 dynamics was associated with the increase in cisplatin-induced γH2AX (Figure 4D and E and Figure 4—figure supplement 2C), the phosphorylated form of the histone H2AX that marks DNA double-strand breaks (Kuo and Yang, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by western blot and chromatin flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4D and E and Figure 4—figure supplement 2C, and citation to Kuo and Yang, 2008.

claim: Mannose challenge did not enhance cisplatin-induced γH2AX in human cancer cell lines that express varying levels of MPI, although mannose challenge significantly suppressed cell proliferation in MPIlow cancer cells.
source: Notably, mannose challenge did not enhance cisplatin-induced γH2AX in human cancer cell lines that express varying levels of MPI, although mannose challenge significantly suppressed cell proliferation in MPIlow cancer cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A–F) as reported previously (Gonzalez et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by western blot and cell proliferation data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3A–F, and citation to Gonzalez et al., 2018.

claim: The endogenous levels of γH2AX were detected in S phase of both mannose-challenged and -unchallenged MPI-KO HT1080 and MPI-KO HeLa cells.
source: The endogenous levels of γH2AX were detected in S phase of both mannose-challenged and -unchallenged MPI-KO HT1080 and MPI-KO HeLa cells (Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 4B)
evidence: This is supported by chromatin flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 4B.

claim: Cisplatin strongly induced γH2AX throughout S phase even in mannose-challenged MPI-KO cancer cells.
source: and cisplatin strongly induced γH2AX throughout S phase even in these mannose-challenged MPI-KO cancer cells (Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This is supported by chromatin flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 4B.

claim: Mannose challenge caused a steep drop of ECAR with a faint increase in OCR, resulting in a marked reduction in ATP production rates.
source: Mannose challenge caused a steep drop of ECAR with a faint increase in OCR (Figure 5A and B), resulting in a marked reduction in ATP production rates (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by Seahorse bioenergetics data shown in Figure 5A, B, and C.

claim: The remaining ECAR further decreased after oligomycin A treatment in mannose-challenged cells, while the same treatment increased ECAR in mannose-unchallenged cells, indicating that mannose challenge ablates glycolytic capacity, which is required to buffer the defects in OXPHOS.
source: The remaining ECAR further decreased after oligomycin A treatment in mannose-challenged cells, while the same treatment increased ECAR in mannose-unchallenged cells (Figure 5A), indicating that mannose challenge ablates glycolytic capacity, which is required to buffer the defects in OXPHOS.
evidence: This is supported by Seahorse bioenergetics data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Mannose challenge decreased the ATP pool in MPI-KO HT1080 cells, MPI-KO HeLa cells, and MPI-KO MEFs.
source: Consistent with these bioenergetic estimations, mannose challenge decreased the ATP pool in MPI-KO HT1080 cells, MPI-KO HeLa cells, and MPI-KO MEFs (Figure 5D and E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B)
evidence: This is supported by ATP assay data shown in Figure 5D and E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: The remaining ATP pool was almost completely depleted by co-treatment with IACS-010759, a preclinical small-molecule inhibitor of complex I of the mitochondrial respiratory chain, which in turn increased necrosis.
source: and the remaining pool was almost completely depleted by co-treatment with IACS-010759, a preclinical small-molecule inhibitor of complex I of the mitochondrial respiratory chain (Molina et al., 2018; Figure 5D and E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B), which in turn increased necrosis (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by ATP assay and LDH release data shown in Figure 5D, E, F, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B, and citation to Molina et al., 2018.

claim: One-day mannose challenge greatly increased the pool of Fruc-6-P, while that of the three-carbon metabolites in the lower glycolysis chain, including lactate, were substantially decreased.
source: One-day mannose challenge greatly increased the pool of Fruc-6-P, while that of the three-carbon metabolites in the lower glycolysis chain, including lactate, were substantially decreased (Figure 5G), supporting our earlier findings that mannose challenge decreased ECAR to the basal level.
evidence: This is supported by metabolomic data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: The steady state levels of metabolites in oxidative and non-oxidative arms of the pentose phosphate pathway (PPP) remained relatively unchanged in the mannose-challenged cells, except for the large accumulation of 6-phosphogluconoate and the slight decrease in sedoheptulose-7-phosphate.
source: Despite this glycolytic alteration, the steady state levels of metabolites in oxidative and non-oxidative arms of the pentose phosphate pathway (PPP) remained relatively unchanged in the mannose-challenged cells, except for the large accumulation of 6-phosphogluconoate and the slight decrease in sedoheptulose-7-phosphate (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is supported by metabolomic data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Mannose challenge severely decreased tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle intermediates (isocitrate, 2-oxoglutarate, succinate, fumarate, and malate) that are used to generate NADH and FADH2 as electron donors for the mitochondrial respiratory chain.
source: In contrast, mannose challenge severely decreased tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle intermediates (isocitrate, 2-oxoglutarate, succinate, fumarate, and malate) that are used to generate NADH and FADH2 as electron donors for the mitochondrial respiratory chain (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by metabolomic data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The amounts of ribonucleoside diphosphates and triphosphates, but not ribonucleoside monophosphates, were proportionally and moderately decreased in mannose-challenged cells.
source: Strikingly, the amounts of ribonucleoside diphosphates and triphosphates, but not ribonucleoside monophosphates, were proportionally and moderately decreased (Figure 5I–K)
evidence: This is supported by metabolomic data shown in Figure 5I–K.

claim: Deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates (dNTPs) were substantially decreased in the mannose-challenged cells.
source: whereas deoxyribonucleoside triphosphates (dNTPs) were substantially decreased in the mannose-challenged cells (Figure 5L).
evidence: This is supported by metabolomic data shown in Figure 5L.

claim: Fractional enrichment of 13C-PRPP (M+5) was saturated at 30 min in unchallenged cells, while it was still in a sub-dynamic labeling phase in mannose-challenged cells.
source: Fractional enrichment of 13C-PRPP (M+5) was saturated at 30 min in unchallenged cells, while it was still in a sub-dynamic labeling phase in mannose-challenged cells (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by 13C-glucose tracing data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The pool size of 13C-PRPP (M+5) in mannose-challenged cells was similar to that in unchallenged cells, implying that mannose challenge reduced the utilization of PRPP for nucleotide biosynthesis.
source: Despite this slower fractional enrichment, the pool size of 13C-PRPP (M+5) in mannose-challenged cells was similar to that in unchallenged cells (Figure 6D), implying that mannose challenge reduced the utilization of PRPP for nucleotide biosynthesis.
evidence: This is supported by 13C-glucose tracing data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: There was a marked reduction in both the fractional enrichment and the pool size of 13C-purine metabolic intermediates (M+5) in mannose-challenged cells, which included inosine-5′-monophosphate (IMP), adenosine-5′-monophosphate (AMP), and guanosine-5′-monophosphate (GMP).
source: Consistent with this assumption, we found a marked reduction in both the fractional enrichment and the pool size of 13C-purine metabolic intermediates (M+5) in mannose-challenged cells, which included inosine-5′-monophosphate (IMP; Figure 6E and F), adenosine-5′-monophosphate (AMP; Figure 6G and H), and guanosine-5′-monophosphate (GMP; Figure 6I and J).
evidence: This is supported by 13C-glucose tracing data shown in Figure 6E–J.

claim: The fractional enrichment and the pool size of 13C-glycine (M+2) largely decreased in mannose-challenged cells, suggesting that the GSF axis is compromised in these cells.
source: However, the fractional enrichment and the pool size of 13C-glycine (M+2) largely decreased in mannose-challenged cells (Figure 6K and L), suggesting that the GSF axis is compromised in these cells.
evidence: This is supported by 13C-glucose tracing data shown in Figure 6K and L.

claim: Mannose challenge severely decreased the fractional enrichment of both 13C-Asp (M+2, M+3, and M+4) and 13C-carbamoyl Asp (M+2, M+3, and M+4).
source: However, mannose challenge severely decreased the fractional enrichment of both 13C-Asp (M+2, M+3, and M+4) and 13C-carbamoyl Asp (M+2, M+3, and M+4) (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B and D).
evidence: This is supported by 13C-glucose tracing data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2B and D.

claim: The pool size of 13C-Asp (M+2) remained relatively unchanged between mannose-challenged and -unchallenged cells, while the pool size of 13C-carbamoyl Asp (M+2) greatly decreased in mannose-challenged cells, indicating that mannose challenge reduced the utilization of Asp in pyrimidine metabolism.
source: In contrast, the pool size of 13C-Asp (M+2) remained relatively unchanged between mannose-challenged and -unchallenged cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C), while the pool size of 13C-carbamoyl Asp (M+2) greatly decreased in mannose-challenged cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 2E), indicating that mannose challenge reduced the utilization of Asp in pyrimidine metabolism.
evidence: This is supported by 13C-glucose tracing data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2C and E.

claim: Mannose-challenged cells showed a substantial reduction of 13C-UMP in both the fractional enrichment (M+5, M+6, M+7, and M+8) and the pool size (M+5), clearly indicating that mannose challenge impaired the biosynthesis of pyrimidine nucleotides.
source: However, mannose-challenged cells showed a substantial reduction of 13C-UMP in both the fractional enrichment (M+5, M+6, M+7, and M+8) and the pool size (M+5) (Figure 6—figure supplement 2I and J), clearly indicating that mannose challenge impaired the biosynthesis of pyrimidine nucleotides.
evidence: This is supported by 13C-glucose tracing data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2I and J.

claim: dNTPs showed little 13C enrichment (dATP and dGTP) and a very low 13C enrichment (dTTP and dCTP) in mannose-challenged cells compared with those in unchallenged cells.
source: As expected, dNTPs showed little 13C enrichment (dATP and dGTP, Figure 6—figure supplement 3A–E) and a very low 13C enrichment (dTTP and dCTP, Figure 6—figure supplement 3F–J) in mannose-challenged cells compared with those in unchallenged cells.
evidence: This is supported by 13C-glucose tracing data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3A–J.

claim: The combination of HU and cisplatin more severely reduced cell viability than cisplatin treatment alone, independently of the presence or absence of the MPI gene.
source: We found that the combination of HU and cisplatin more severely reduced cell viability than cisplatin treatment alone, independently of the presence or absence of the MPI gene (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by cell viability assay data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The chemosensitizing effect of HU was associated with the strong induction of γH2AX.
source: This chemosensitizing effect of HU was associated with the strong induction of γH2AX (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: HU treatment at a moderate concentration (0.25 mM) resulted in the arrest of cells in the early to late S phase, while a higher concentration of HU (1 mM) almost completely arrested the cells at the G1/S boundary.
source: Profiling of the chromatin-bound MCM2 showed that HU treatment at a moderate concentration (0.25 mM) resulted in the arrest of cells in the early to late S phase, while a higher concentration of HU (1 mM) almost completely arrested the cells at the G1/S boundary (Figure 7C), partly recapitulating the inhibitory effects of mannose challenge on cell cycle progression.
evidence: This is supported by chromatin flow cytometry data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The forced activation of dormant origins by ATRi failed to increase BrdU uptake in the presence of HU, indicating that the DNA synthesis from dormant origins is highly sensitive to the pool size of dNTPs.
source: As with the case of mannose challenge, the forced activation of dormant origins by ATRi failed to increase BrdU uptake in the presence of HU (Figure 7D–G), indicating that the DNA synthesis from dormant origins is highly sensitive to the pool size of dNTPs.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 7D–G.

claim: HU treatment did not severely impair the CDC45 unloading/reloading dynamics during replication stress, indicating that the insufficient dNTP pool is a major cause of the disengagement of dormant origins from DNA synthesis.
source: Unlike mannose challenge, however, HU treatment did not severely impair the CDC45 unloading/reloading dynamics during replication stress (Figure 7G), indicating that the insufficient dNTP pool is a major cause of the disengagement of dormant origins from DNA synthesis.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 7G.

claim: The conversion of Man-6-P to Fruc-6-P mediated by MPI is critical to directing the excess Man-6-P to glycolysis.
source: In contrast, the conversion of Man-6-P to Fruc-6-P mediated by the same enzyme is critical to directing the excess Man-6-P to glycolysis, while the cellular function of this seemingly wasteful metabolic pathway has long remained unknown.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by the overall findings of the study.

claim: The conversion of Man-6-P to Fruc-6-P mediated by MPI functions as a genome guard through the maintenance of metabolic integrity, which could be threatened by dietary mannose intake.
source: These findings shed light on the conversion of Man-6-P to Fruc-6-P mediated by MPI as a genome guard through the maintenance of metabolic integrity, which could be threatened by dietary mannose intake.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: The induction of ATP insufficiency by honeybee syndrome coincided with that of abnormal cell cycle progression, indicating the critical role of normal mannose catabolism in balancing bioenergetic states and cell cycle progression.
source: The induction of ATP insufficiency by honeybee syndrome coincided with that of abnormal cell cycle progression, indicating the critical role of normal mannose catabolism in balancing bioenergetic states and cell cycle progression.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: The antiproliferative effect of mannose is largely dependent on the expression levels of MPI.
source: An examination of human cancer cell lines that express varying levels of MPI clearly indicated that the antiproliferative effect of mannose is largely dependent on the expression levels of MPI, while mannose-driven genomic instability is a unique phenotype observed in the absence of MPI.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Mannose-driven genomic instability is a unique phenotype observed in the absence of MPI.
source: An examination of human cancer cell lines that express varying levels of MPI clearly indicated that the antiproliferative effect of mannose is largely dependent on the expression levels of MPI, while mannose-driven genomic instability is a unique phenotype observed in the absence of MPI.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: DNA synthesis from dormant origins during replication stress is highly sensitive to the dNTP pool size.
source: Our finding that DNA synthesis from dormant origins during replication stress is highly sensitive to the dNTP pool size is in good agreement with the therapeutic advantages of RNR inhibition in enhancing the efficacy of radiochemotherapy (Kunos and Ivy, 2018).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings and supported by citation to Kunos and Ivy, 2018.

claim: Mannose challenge rapidly increases the expression of RRM2B, which is a rate-limiting and TP53-inducible subunit of RNR.
source: Our proteomic analysis revealed that mannose challenge rapidly increases the expression of RRM2B (Source data 1), which is a rate-limiting and TP53-inducible subunit of RNR (Håkansson et al., 2006; Tanaka et al., 2000), indicating that the equilibrium of dNTP metabolism shifted toward biosynthesis at the protein level.
evidence: This is supported by proteomic data in Source data 1 and citations to Håkansson et al., 2006 and Tanaka et al., 2000.

claim: Mannose challenge caused substantial reductions in the pool of ATP, which is a key allosteric regulator for the catalysis of RNR to occur.
source: However, mannose challenge caused substantial reductions in the pool of ATP, which is a key allosteric regulator for the catalysis of RNR to occur (Brignole et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by ATP assay data and citation to Brignole et al., 2018.

claim: Mannose challenge severely impairs the early stages of de novo synthesis of purine and pyrimidine nucleotides.
source: Our [13C6]-glucose tracer experiments clearly indicated that mannose challenge severely impairs the early stages of de novo synthesis of purine and pyrimidine nucleotides.
evidence: This is supported by 13C-glucose tracing data shown in Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplements.

claim: Fueling the salvage pathway of purine and pyrimidine metabolism with hypoxanthine and thymidine or with deoxyribonucleoside mixture was not sufficient to improve the defects in proliferation of mannose-challenged MPI-KO HT1080 cells.
source: Fueling the salvage pathway of purine and pyrimidine metabolism with hypoxanthine and thymidine (Figure 6—figure supplement 4A) or with deoxyribonucleoside mixture (Figure 6—figure supplement 4B) was not sufficient to improve the defects in proliferation of mannose-challenged MPI-KO HT1080 cells.
evidence: This is supported by cell proliferation data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 4A and B.

claim: The downregulation of MCM2-7 proteins in mannose-challenged cells supports the hypothesis that honeybee syndrome impairs dormant origins and causes genomic instability.
source: The downregulation of MCM2-7 proteins in mannose-challenged cells supports our hypothesis that honeybee syndrome impairs dormant origins and causes genomic instability (Ibarra et al., 2008; Kawabata et al., 2011; Shima et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by proteomic data and citations to Ibarra et al., 2008, Kawabata et al., 2011, and Shima et al., 2007.

claim: Mannose challenge upregulated proteins involved in ferroptosis and necroptosis.
source: Moreover, mannose challenge upregulated proteins involved in ferroptosis and necroptosis.
evidence: This is supported by proteomic data shown in Figure 3A.
